title: The Supreme Court First Gave Students Constitutional Rights, Then Gave Back Searches and Paddlings
dek: From refusing to salute the flag to searching backpacks, six cases gradually map out the constitutional rights of American public school students; the Supreme Court, while declaring that "schools are not totalitarian enclaves," also upheld corporal punishment and searches based on reasonable suspicion, thereby narrowing the boundaries of those rights.
why: Each case is explained in five or six minutes, covering background and key rulings—ideal for listeners who want to grasp the boundaries of speech, corporal punishment, and backpack searches in American public schools in one go.
who: Parents, middle and high school teachers, and law students, as well as anyone wanting to understand the boundary between government power and children's rights in American public schools.
skip: Listeners familiar with the Establishment Clause can skip the second case; those who know the earlier cases well can jump to the corporal punishment and search cases after 25:40.

points.h: Flag-salute case: student rights enter the schoolhouse
points.body: Can students really claim First Amendment rights during class? This case actually began with religion: Jehovah's Witnesses families believed saluting the flag violated the commandments against other gods and idolatry, so they refused to salute or pledge. In 1940, the Supreme Court ruled against them, and World War II led more districts to require daily salutes and pledges. West Virginia expelled students who refused to recite the pledge, labeled them delinquents, and parents could be fined or jailed. In 1943, the Supreme Court reversed 6–3, with Justice Jackson writing on Flag Day: no official can define orthodoxy in politics, nationalism, religion, or other opinions; students need not confess words that contradict their hearts or make empty gestures. This was the first time the Court established that students have some First Amendment rights inside school.

points.h: Official prayer struck down as unconstitutional
points.body: During the Cold War, America cast itself as a God-fearing nation, adding "Under God" to the Pledge in 1954, and more public schools began reading scripture or praying before class. In 1951, the New York State Board of Regents asked religious leaders to compose a short, interdenominational prayer, leaving adoption to local districts. Districts that used it allowed students to opt out, but parents of ten students sued anyway. In 1962, Engel v. Vitale ruled 6–1 that it was unconstitutional—not because it was mandatory, but because the prayer was written by the government, which itself constituted an establishment of religion. Justice Black quoted Madison: "It is proper to take alarm at the first experiment on our liberties"; the same power that could establish Christianity to the exclusion of other religions could easily establish one sect of Christianity. The decision sparked fierce backlash, and the plaintiff families faced ridicule and harassment.

In December 1965, Des Moines middle and high school students planned to wear black armbands to class to protest US involvement in Vietnam. School officials announced in advance that those who refused to remove them would be suspended, yet some students—including four siblings—wore them and were suspended. In 1969, the Supreme Court ruled 7–2 for the students. The issue was not ordinary dress code but a quiet, passive expression close to pure speech, and it did not disrupt class. Without evidence of actual or reasonably foreseeable material disruption of schoolwork, school officials could not suppress student opinion. The opinion declared: "It can hardly be argued that either students or teachers shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech or expression at the schoolhouse gate." This "substantial disruption" test became the benchmark for campus speech. Justice Black dissented, predicting students would defy nearly all rules; the hosts note that this slippery-slope argument sounds quite absurd.

In 1983, Hazelwood East High School's student newspaper, The Spectrum, had two articles that troubled Principal Reynolds: one on teenage pregnancy used pseudonyms but might still identify the interviewee, and a divorce story named and criticized a student's parent. Reynolds decided to delete the entire two pages rather than just the articles, citing lack of time to edit and the need to publish before semester's end. In 1988, the Supreme Court ruled 5–3 for the school. The key distinction was between "tolerating student speech" and "promoting student speech": the paper was funded by the school, readers would assume school endorsement, and the two pieces were indeed immature in journalistic ethics. The Court held that schools may regulate content they promote. This drew the first clear boundary around Tinker's rights.

points.h: Corporal punishment is not cruel and unusual
points.body: Host Tracy suddenly recalled that many teachers kept wooden paddles on their desks when she was young, and research showed corporal punishment has not disappeared in the US. In the 1977 case Ingram v. Wright, the school's paddle was less than two feet long, three to four inches wide, and half an inch thick, with a stated maximum of one to five swats; but Ingram received more than 20 swats in a single incident and required medical attention. The Supreme Court did not dwell on whether this particular case was excessive; it ruled that school corporal punishment does not violate the Constitution. The Eighth Amendment protects convicted persons; prisoners and schoolchildren are separated by "the harsh fact of criminal conviction and incarceration." Schools are open institutions, with teachers and classmates as witnesses, and students go home at the end of the day. According to NEA statistics, corporal punishment remains legal in public schools in 17 states, actually practiced in 14, with boys, Black students, and disabled students paddled at significantly higher rates.

points.h: Backpack search needs only reasonable suspicion
points.body: In 1980, a 14-year-old New Jersey student, TLO, was reported by a teacher for smoking in the bathroom. Vice Principal Choplik searched her purse, found cigarettes and rolling papers, then continued digging and found what appeared to be marijuana and evidence of drug dealing. TLO was convicted and sentenced to one year of probation. In 1985, the Supreme Court ruled 6–3 that the search was legal. The Court acknowledged that the Fourth Amendment applies to school officials and that students have a legitimate expectation of privacy, but it must be balanced against the school's need to maintain a learning environment. Therefore, school searches need not meet the probable cause standard required for police; a lower threshold of reasonable suspicion suffices. The teacher's report gave the vice principal reason to suspect she had cigarettes, and the purse was the obvious place; seeing rolling papers naturally extended suspicion to marijuana, which was also reasonable.

Students in school as well as out of school are persons under our Constitution.
